replacement: “Great elder, tell me! Does my liveliness annoy you?” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried suddenly. He gripped the arms of his chair with both hands, as if he meant to jump up if the answer was a bad one.

“Entirely at home? To be my natural self? Oh, that’s much too much, but I take it with grateful joy. You know, blessed Father, you’d better not invite me to be my natural self. Don’t risk it.... I won’t go so far myself. I’m warning you for your own good. As for the rest, it’s still lost in the mists of uncertainty, though there are people who’d be delighted to describe me to you. I mean that for you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. But you, holy being, I tell you, I’m simply overflowing with ecstasy.”

“No, not about Diderot. Above all, do not lie to yourself. A man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to a point where he cannot tell the truth in himself or around him, and so he loses all respect for himself and for others. Having no respect, he stops loving. And to keep himself occupied and distracted without love, he gives himself up to passions and coarse pleasures, and in his vices he sinks to the level of a beast. All of this comes from lying continually to other men and to himself. The man who lies to himself can be more easily offended than anyone. You know, it is sometimes very pleasant to take offense, is it not? A man may know that no one has insulted him, that he has invented the insult himself, lied and exaggerated to make it picturesque, seized on one word and made a mountain out of a molehill. He knows all this, and still he is the first to take offense. He revels in his resentment until it gives him great pleasure, and so he passes to real vindictiveness. But get up, sit down, please. All this, too, is deceitful posturing....”

The elder suddenly stood up. “Excuse me, gentlemen, if I leave you for a few minutes,” he said to all his guests. “There are visitors waiting for me who came before you. But do not tell lies all the same,” he added to Fyodor Pavlovitch, with a good-humored face. He left the cell, and Alyosha and the novice hurried after him to escort him down the steps. Alyosha was out of breath. He was glad to get away, but glad too that the elder was in good humor and not offended. Father Zossima was heading for the portico to bless the people waiting there. But Fyodor Pavlovitch stubbornly stopped him at the door of the cell.

Father Zossima came into the portico and went first straight to the peasants, who were crowded at the bottom of the three steps up to it. He stood on the top step, put on his stole, and began blessing the women as they pressed around him. A crazy woman was brought up to him. The moment she saw the elder, she began to shriek and writhe as if in the pains of childbirth. He laid the stole on her forehead and said a short prayer over her, and at once she grew calm and quiet.

I do not know how it is now, but in my childhood I often saw and heard these “possessed” women in villages and monasteries. They were brought to mass, and there they would squeal and bark like dogs so loudly that the whole church heard them. But when the sacrament was carried in and they were led up to it, the “possession” stopped at once, and for a while the sick women were always calm. As a child I was deeply impressed and amazed by this. Then I heard from our country neighbors and from my teachers in town that the whole illness was faked to get out of work, and that it could always be cured by suitable severity. They told various stories to prove it. Later, though, medical specialists told me, to my astonishment, that nothing is faked here. It is a terrible illness that women suffer from, and it is especially widespread among us in Russia. It comes, they said, from the hard lot of peasant women. A woman goes back to exhausting work too soon after a difficult, unnatural childbirth with no help. Add hopeless misery and beatings and the like, which some women could not bear as well as others. The strange, instant cure of the frantic, struggling woman as soon as she was brought to the holy sacrament had been explained to me as malingering and the trickery of the “clericals.” In fact, it probably came about in the most natural way. The women who held her up, and the sick woman herself, were completely certain that the evil spirit inside her could not hold out once she was brought to the sacrament and made to bow down before it. So in a nervous, mentally disturbed woman, the whole body always went into a sort of convulsion, and it was bound to, at the moment of bowing down. The expectation of a miraculous cure and the unquestioning belief that it would come set it off. And it did come, though only for a moment. It was exactly the same now, as soon as the elder touched the sick woman with the stole.
